messages.author: 84d40346d2b44e80
messages.subject: Regression line exceeds confidence band
parts:
Hi All,
 
I don't recall a regression line in ggplot2 exceeding the shaded confidence band, but that's what happened in the attached plot. Is this normal, and if so, under what conditions does it happen? The smallest x value is a bit of an outlier, so perhaps that's what causes it. Here's the code that did it:
 
# Create a function to apply by group
my_ggplot <- function(x) {
  print(
    ggplot(x, aes(pretest,posttest)) +
      geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm) +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = my_xlim) +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = my_ylim) +
      labs(title = unique(x$workshop) )
) }
 
and my_xlim was set to 58 86 to standardize the axes across groups. I'm using ggplot2 0.9.3 and plyr 1.8.
 
Thanks,
Bob

messages.author: fd4f3538f907404b
messages.subject: Re: Regression line exceeds confidence band
parts:
Because you set the limits with scale_y_continuous, the lowermost
segment of the confidence interval (which would transgress the minimum
y-bound) is getting clipped. This is standard (if sometimes annoying)
behaviour ... you can either use coord_cartesian() to set the limits, or
library(scales); scale_y_continuous(limits = my_ylim, oob = squish) ...

Ben Bolker

messages.subject: Re: Regression line exceeds confidence band
parts:

instead of those two scale_continuous calls.

Ben

messages.author: 84d40346d2b44e80
messages.subject: Re: Regression line exceeds confidence band
parts:
Hi Ben,
 
Those were both useful suggestions. The coord_cartesian worked, but it was so precise that it displayed only 1/4 of the extreme point! At first I didn't even realize that the point was there at all. It is almost invisible in the lower left corner. I used a paint package to add an arrow & some text so people would see it. 
 
The squish setting from the scales package did much better, showing the whole point and a bit of axis beyond it. Very nice!  Both plots are attached.
 
From help(squish) I never would have guessed it would have this effect. The examples are rather mysterious. Is the oob argument documented anywhere?
 
 
Thanks!
Bob
